feedback.pattern: Missing ConcurrentModificationException detection in tree modification
feedback.explanation: This test has failed consistently since run 45 when the remove() method was first implemented. The code diffs from runs 45–51 show changes focused on the core remove() logic (handling return values, size counts, and edge cases), with no modifications to iterator state tracking or concurrent modification detection. The test expects a ConcurrentModificationException to be thrown when the tree is modified (via remove()) while an iterator is actively traversing it. The iterator implementation currently contains no mechanism to detect or report such modifications. The remove() method's core functionality was corrected by run 55, bringing 34 of 39 tests to pass, but this test remains unresolved because it requires a different feature: tracking modification counts in the tree and validating them in the iterator's next() method.
nextSteps: Implement a modification counter in the BST class that increments every time the tree structure changes (insert, remove). Store the counter value in each iterator when it is created, then check before each next() call whether the current counter matches the stored value—if not, throw ConcurrentModificationException.

Review the iterator's next() method to ensure it validates the modification counter at the start of each iteration step, not just at iterator creation. This prevents modifications that occur mid-traversal from going undetected.

Test the modification counter logic by manually modifying the tree (adding or removing nodes) between iterator creation and iteration, verifying that the exception is raised at the correct point in the iteration cycle.

feedback.pattern: Missing IllegalStateException for iterator.remove() without preceding next()
feedback.explanation: This test has failed consistently since run 45 and remains unresolved through run 57. It was introduced when remove() was first implemented, but the code diffs from runs 49–55 show changes focused on fixing the core remove() method's logic and return values. The test expects an IllegalStateException when iterator.remove() is called without a preceding next() call, or when next() has not been called at all. The iterator implementation currently lacks state tracking to distinguish between 'just created', 'positioned after next()', and 'remove already called' states. This requires adding a flag to track whether next() has been called since the last remove() or since iterator creation.
nextSteps: Add a boolean flag to each iterator (e.g., canRemove) that is set to true only after next() successfully returns a value, and reset to false after remove() is called. Check this flag at the start of remove() and throw IllegalStateException if it is false.

Ensure the flag is properly initialized to false when the iterator is created, and that it is reset to false after a successful remove() to prevent consecutive remove() calls without an intervening next().

Combine this state tracking with the modification counter check from the concurrent modification test: both validations should occur in the iterator's remove() method before any tree modification happens.

feedback.pattern: Missing ConcurrentModificationException detection in iterator traversal
feedback.explanation: This test has failed since run 45 when remove() was introduced, and remains unresolved through run 57. The code diffs from runs 45–55 show changes directed at fixing the core remove() method's correctness (return values, size tracking, edge cases), not at adding concurrency detection to iterators. The test expects a ConcurrentModificationException to be thrown when the underlying tree is modified (via tree.remove()) while an iterator is in the middle of traversal. The iterator currently contains no mechanism to detect that the tree has changed, because there is no shared modification counter between the tree and its iterators. This requires adding a modification tracking mechanism to the BST class and having each iterator validate it before proceeding.
nextSteps: Implement a modification counter field in the BST class (e.g., modCount) that increments whenever insert() or remove() modifies the tree structure. This counter should be incremented before the modification completes, so any iterator created before the change will have a different stored value.

In each iterator's constructor, capture the current modCount value. Before each call to next(), verify that the stored modCount still equals the tree's current modCount; if not, throw ConcurrentModificationException with a clear message.

Test by creating an iterator, calling next() a few times, then calling tree.remove() directly (not through the iterator), then attempting to call next() again on the iterator—this should raise the exception.

feedback.pattern: Missing IllegalStateException for iterator.remove() without preceding next()
feedback.explanation: This test has failed consistently since run 45 and remains unresolved through run 57. It was introduced alongside the other concurrency tests when remove() was first implemented, but the code diffs from runs 49–55 show changes focused exclusively on fixing the core remove() method's logic and return values. The test expects an IllegalStateException when the iterator's remove() method is called without a preceding next() call. The iterator currently lacks the state tracking needed to enforce this precondition. This iterator-level validation requires a separate mechanism: a flag that tracks whether next() has been called since the iterator was created or since the last remove() call.
nextSteps: Add a state flag to the iterator (e.g., lastOperationWasNext) that is initialized to false and set to true only when next() successfully returns a value. In the iterator's remove() method, check this flag and throw IllegalStateException if it is false.
Reset the flag to false after remove() completes, ensuring that consecutive remove() calls without an intervening next() are also rejected.
Combine this check with the modification counter validation: both should be performed in the iterator's remove() method, with the state check happening first (before any tree modification).

feedback.pattern: Missing ConcurrentModificationException detection in pre-order iterator
feedback.explanation: This test has failed since run 45 and remains unresolved through run 57. It is one of five concurrency-related tests that were introduced when remove() was first implemented. The code diffs from runs 45–55 show changes directed at fixing the core remove() method's functionality (return values, size counts, edge cases), not at adding concurrency detection to the pre-order iterator. The test expects a ConcurrentModificationException when the tree is modified (via tree.remove()) while a pre-order iterator is actively traversing. The pre-order iterator, like the in-order iterator, currently contains no mechanism to detect tree modifications because there is no shared modification counter between the tree and its iterators. This requires adding a modification counter in the BST class that both iterators can check.
nextSteps: Implement a modification counter in the BST class that increments on every insert() and remove() call. Have each iterator (both in-order and pre-order) capture this counter value at creation time.

In the pre-order iterator's next() method, validate that the captured counter still matches the tree's current counter before returning the next element. If they differ, throw ConcurrentModificationException.
Verify that the pre-order iterator's traversal logic (which typically uses a stack-based approach) correctly detects modifications at each step, not just at the start of iteration.

feedback.pattern: Regression in remove() return value logic, resolved through iterative debugging
feedback.explanation: This test passed at run 50 after initially failing at run 45 when remove() was first implemented. A regression occurred at run 53 when the remove() logic was rewritten, causing the test to fail with incorrect size counts (expected 4 but got 14). Run 54 made the situation worse with inverted expectations and a StackOverflowError. The code diffs show that run 50 removed 5 lines and added 1, run 53 removed 10 lines and added 6, and run 55 removed 19 lines and added 19. The test now passes as of run 55. The regression cycle (runs 53–54) shows that the remove() implementation required comprehensive reconsideration across all scenarios (leaf nodes, nodes with one child, nodes with two children, and root removal).
nextSteps: Review the final remove() implementation to understand how it correctly handles all four node removal cases: leaf nodes (no children), nodes with only a left child, nodes with only a right child, and nodes with two children. Pay special attention to how the size counter is updated in each case.

For future tree modifications, create a test matrix covering all removal scenarios before making changes: test removing from an empty tree, removing a leaf, removing a node with one child on each side, removing a node with two children, and removing the root in each configuration. This prevents regressions like run 53.

When a regression occurs (test passes, then fails after a rewrite), compare the old working version with the new broken version side-by-side to identify which case(s) the new logic handles incorrectly, rather than making incremental patches.

feedback.explanation: This test failed at run 45 when remove() was first implemented, passed at run 50 after a fix (5 lines removed, 1 added), then regressed at run 53 when the remove() logic was rewritten (10 lines removed, 6 added). The regression was resolved at run 55 with a complete rewrite (19 lines removed, 19 added). Runs 47–48 show isolated test executions of testRemove only. The test now passes as of run 57. The pattern shows an initial implementation, a quick fix, a larger rewrite that introduced a regression, and finally a complete reimplementation that restored correctness. This mirrors the behavior of testRemoveReturnValue, indicating both tests required comprehensive reconsideration of the remove() logic.
nextSteps: Understand the three-case structure of BST node removal: (1) node is a leaf—simply remove it; (2) node has one child—replace it with that child; (3) node has two children—find the in-order successor (or predecessor), replace the node's value with the successor's value, and recursively remove the successor. Ensure your implementation handles all three cases correctly.

When testing remove(), verify that the tree's size is correctly decremented and that the tree structure remains valid (all left descendants are smaller, all right descendants are larger) after each removal. Use a helper method to validate tree invariants after each operation.

If a rewrite of remove() causes regressions, revert to the last passing version and make smaller, more targeted changes rather than rewriting the entire method. Test each change in isolation before moving to the next.
